Generative AI systems increasingly mediate how researchers encounter and make sense of scholarly information. By producing coherent explanations from multiple sources, these systems may influence how users assess their understanding, evaluate supporting evidence, and decide whether further investigation is necessary. This project investigates how AI-generated scholarly synthesis shapes judgments of explanatory and evidentiary sufficiency in academic research. Its central question is whether, and under what conditions, the perceived completeness of an explanation influences a researcher’s assessment of the evidence supporting it and their decision to continue or conclude an information search. The research draws on library and information science, human-computer interaction, epistemology, and cognitive psychology. It examines established accounts of information satisficing, search stopping behavior, cognitive authority, epistemic dependence, and metacognitive calibration to assess how these concepts explain information-seeking decisions in AI-mediated environments. A central distinction concerns the difference between understanding an explanation and having sufficient grounds to accept its claims. These judgments may coincide, but they need not. An explanation may adequately address a research question while leaving important uncertainties about source quality, methodological limitations, or competing interpretations unresolved. Conversely, reliance on a well-supported synthesis may be entirely justified without extensive examination of every underlying source. Rather than treating reduced information seeking as an inherent failure, the project considers how researchers determine when further inquiry is warranted. It examines the conditions under which AI-generated synthesis may support well-calibrated judgments, encourage critical engagement with evidence, or contribute to premature conclusions. The project aims to develop a theoretically grounded account of evidentiary judgment and inquiry termination in AI-mediated scholarly research, with implications for information literacy, scholarly information practices, and the design of research support systems.

Why does meaningful work become inaccessible to certain groups? Existing literature increasingly recognizes that access to meaningful work is shaped by both subjective experiences and objective conditions, yet it remains less clear about how and why such access becomes systematically constrained. In particular, prior studies tend to foreground workers’ active agency in engaging with, negotiating or resisting these conditions of meaningful work, but they offer limited insight into how this capacity itself may be restricted. Drawing on Archer’s distinction between active and passive agency, we conceptualize passive agency as a mechanism through which structural constraints limit workers’ capability for purposive action. Based on 33 interviews with disabled workers in China, we show how ableism acts as a structural constraint, positioning disabled workers as passive agents, restricting their capacity to experience work as meaningful by limiting opportunities for autonomy, dignity and recognition. In doing so, we extend current understanding of meaningful work by specifying how structural constraints give rise to passive agency, thereby systematically foreclosing access to meaningful work. We also clarify contingent conditions under which more active forms of agency may be enacted, and thus meaningful work can be sustained.

Scholars have proposed ethical principles and frameworks to support industry practitioners developing responsible AI. To enable these from theory to practice, a subset of research explores how practitioners actually enact abstract ethical concepts and guidance, surfacing factors that limit their efforts—e.g., organizational support—and informing ways to strengthen efforts towards safe and ethical AI in practice—e.g., practical checklists, educational workbooks. Curiously, this has been underexplored in relation to practitioners curating ethical datasets, the very foundation needed for fair ML technologies, despite the existence of various data ethics principles. It is unsurprising, then, that reports continue to emerge of ML datasets curated through questionable practices, including non-consensual web-scraping and exploitative labor practices. To address this gap, we describe the experiences of a project team curating FHIBE: a fair, human-centric benchmark dataset for computer vision technologies, grounded in recommendations by data ethics and fair ML scholars. Using an ethnographic lens, we share the team’s motivation and the set of principles FHIBE was based on, the challenges team members faced trying to execute multiple principles at once, and the ways they adapted in lieu of resources or insights from preceding scholarship. By tracing one team’s end-to-end data curation efforts, we offer new insights into practitioners’ realities translating data ethics, to inform valuable avenues for HCI and policy researchers to address in the future.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Joint displays, which set quantitative and qualitative findings side by side, have become a standard device for integrating results in mixed-methods research. In practice, researchers tend to report convergence and to explain away divergence by attributing it to a weakness in one strand. This methodological paper argues that divergence is frequently the most informative product of a joint display and shows how it can be used to refine a practical framework. The argument is developed through a worked example from a mixed-methods study of expatriate educator retention in international high schools in Guangzhou, China, in which a survey of 52 educators was integrated with written interviews with 11. Ten domains were classified as convergent, complementary, divergent or qualitative only: five converged, three were complementary, one diverged and one emerged only in the interviews.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping higher education, yet many students still use AI at a basic level and lack a systematic approach to designing learning games in collaboration with AI. This study, the first phase of a research and development (R&D) project, aimed 1) to examine the current conditions and priority developmental needs regarding AI literacy and game design skills among higher education students, and 2) to synthesize a design framework for human–AI collaborative game-based learning innovation. A survey was combined with bibliometric mapping and content synthesis. The survey sample comprised 78 undergraduate students in Computer Education, selected through purposive sampling from a population of 128 students; the document dataset consisted of 31 publications retrieved from Scopus and OpenAlex after deduplication. Survey data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, and instrument reliability was acceptable (Cronbach’s a = 0.89). Document data were analyzed through bibliometric mapping and content synthesis using bibliometrix (R) and VOSviewer. The findings indicated that students’ AI literacy (M = 3.09, SD = 0.83) and game design skills (M = 2.95, SD = 0.90) were at a moderate level, while developmental needs were high (M = 4.14, SD = 0.62), particularly for a systematic AI-supported design approach (M = 4.21, SD = 0.58). The synthesis yielded a six-component design framework covering learner-experience-first design, AI role definition, iterative evidence-based design, MDA mapping, ethical reflection, and prompt preparation. The framework offers an empirical basis for designing learning innovation that integrates AI literacy, game design, and responsible human–AI collaboration, and it guides the development phase of the project.

We present a qualitative interview study with 17 Canadian computer science and software engineering undergraduates exploring their self-initiated, unsupervised AI chatbot use. We find that most participants, despite being CS students often assumed to have stronger technical intuitions, lacked an accurate understanding of how generative AI produces output. This miscalibration was associated with plausibility-based fact-checking: participants who described genAI as a retrieval or database system had no reliable trigger for verifying confidently-stated misinformation. We discuss implications for AI literacy education and human-AI interaction design.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: When an AI agent proposes an action, the user’s decision may be reduced to a brief approval step. A misleading summary can obscure consequences at that point. We propose a protective agent architecture for web browsing and agent approvals intended to inform the user’s decision without exercising authority over it. The design combines on-device estimates of behavioral deviation with deterministic intervention rules specified by the user in advance. Interventions would preserve existing choices while adjusting visual emphasis, exposing omitted information, and adding options. For agent approvals, an independent channel would compare the request with the proposed action’s tool-call arguments. A web-browsing prototype is available; the approval layer and empirical evaluation remain future work. We describe its mechanisms, an illustrative approval scenario, and an evaluation plan, including the unresolved relationship between behavioral deviation and supervisory bandwidth.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Analysts, athletes and coaches have long relied upon decision support tools, but new AI capabilities raise questions of whether they can “appropriately rely” on these models. In this work, we explore the starting lineup decisions of fantasy American football managers in the presence of projected points. Across more than 2.5 million lineup-weeks from a single fantasy platform during the 2025 NFL season, we find that fantasy managers’ starting lineups appropriately rely on AI advice in only 15.8% to 26.8% of cases. Despite managers’ observed near complete reliance, limited deviation from AI advice is often harmful to their decision-making. Bridging literature from critical data studies and AI reliance, we discuss possible explanations for this behavior, and offer design directions towards complementarity in this setting. Finally, we highlight tensions revealed by the case of fantasy football, and invite researchers to consider SportsHCI as a site to bridge social desirability and technical possibility in and beyond sports.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: AI agents now work alongside people in domains ranging from autonomous vehicles to conversational systems. A recurring question is when an agent’s behavior counts as self-determined rather than merely reactive to its human partner. This matters for ethical conduct, which is widely argued to require some form of autonomy. Yet, its computational meaning is rarely made precise. In this paper, we study an agent’s autonomy in dyadic interactions, measured by the extent to which the agent’s behavior is explained by its own state rather than by its partner’s signals. This quantity captures information-theoretic self-determination as inferred from interaction traces. We characterize autonomy as a function of how deterministically the agent acts, how strongly it optimizes payoffs, and how much past interaction it retains. Using analytical and numerical results from four distinct games, we find that autonomy peaks at high but sub-maximal determinism and is dissociable from rationality. All four settings achieve the same level of autonomy regardless of the agent’s payoff disposition, so rationality never raises the ceiling. What the payoff structure determines is the direction in which rationality trades against determinism. Payoff-seeking play economizes on determinism in one setting, payoff-avoiding play in another, and neither matters where the agent cannot influence its payoff. Our results suggest design principles for interactive agents that remain consistent and self-determined.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a part of every organisation's day-to-day operations and is a factor in the way work is being assigned, done, directed and checked. Discussions about this change have primarily been around automation, efficiency and jobs, but also about how an employee's sense of security, competence in their role, independence and sense of identity at work is affected by AI. In this article, we delve into the interconnections between employees' attitudes toward AI, their feelings of job insecurity, and workplace identity. The study was of qualitative, interpretive, documentary design and secondary data analysis was done using reflexive thematic analysis (RTA) based on peer reviewed studies, systematic reviews and reports of international organizations such as ILO and OECD. The five interrelated themes were: (1) Ambivalence about the use of AI: some experiences it as a tool to augment their work while others worry about being monitored, deskilled, and displaced; (2) Anticipatory fear of loss: fear of job loss can occur even if the number of jobs does not decrease; (3) Remediated and reinforced professional identity: when AI is used to complement their job, it enhances their sense of competence, while when it digitises their core job, it threatens it; (4) Algorithmic management reconfigures autonomy: when automating parts of their job, employees' autonomy is reassigned, while when parts of their job are kept by humans and coded into algorithms, they lose some autonomy; (5) Algorithmic management experiences depend on the organizational support, the transparency of communication, participation, and reskilling. From a theoretical perspective, the study synthesizes the concepts of job insecurity, social and/or organizational identification, technology acceptance and resistance, sociotechnical systems and human capital, and is able to articulate a framework beyond the deterministic replacement stories. The reality is that HR teams and leaders need to approach the integration of AI as a transformational journey rather than simply a technological fix, and have to do so. It concludes by proposing that although the technical difficulty is a consideration, a more important one is how well staff can feel secure, competent and valued as professionals in the context of the integration of AI.

BIM adoption in non-mandated emerging economies is a complex sociotechnical process where organizational culture, institutional frameworks, and cognitive dynamics interact. Current literature remains fragmented, evaluating macro-level organizational maturity or micro-level student technology acceptance in isolation, thereby lacking an integrative framework to model how structural governance conditions individual acceptance and perpetuates the digital gap. Addressing this theoretical gap, this study operationalizes an integrated Technology Organization Environment (TOE) and Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) framework. Using non-parametric inferential analysis across AECO organizations (n = 74) and academic-professional stakeholders (n = 71) in Ecuador, findings reveal that despite basic 3D adoption (68.92%), severe governance deficits persist: 51.35% lack defined BIM roles, 66.22% lack training plans, and only 17.57% utilize ISO 19650-compliant Common Data Environments (CDE). High Perceived Usefulness (PU = 62.86%) and learning intention (BIU = 94.20%) are constrained by low Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU), tied to a 58.57% 2D CAD reliance. Inferential testing confirmed macro-organizational factors drive individual acceptance (p < 0.01) and revealed a significant inverse alignment between market demands and learning outcomes (rs = −0.62, p < 0.001). Beyond practical Project-Based Learning (PBL) applications, this study’s primary theoretical contribution establishes a validated baseline identifying PEOU as the core cognitive-operational bottleneck during technological transitions.

Generative AI (genAI) co-produces the work of hundreds of millions of people. Humanoversight, the default safeguard in AI governance, assumes that people still feel responsiblefor the outputs they approve. Yet genAI assistance can lower psychological ownership ofsuch outputs, and whether the resulting loss of felt responsibility can be repaired remainsunclear. Drawing on the triangle model of responsibility and psychological ownership theory,we propose that psychological ownership is how people experience the causal link betweenthemselves and an outcome, that genAI assistance weakens this link, and that a mandatoryverification step after generation can rebuild it. We derive five hypotheses on the erosion andrestoration of psychological ownership and felt responsibility and on revision after criticism,and we outline a 3 × 2 experiment to test them.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Academic advisors increasingly face heavy workloads driven by rising student demand. Designing AI-driven administrative systems based on users’ needs can help alleviate this burden. Our study examines how the perception of human needs and characteristics of communication are affected when AI systems replace human advisors in academic settings. This study employed a mixed-methods design with semi-structured interviews (N = 31) and pre-post surveys (N = 119) to investigate user needs and validate findings for an academic agent-based support system. Our findings show a selective pattern: shifting to AI agents produced significant declines in competence, relatedness, and impactfulness, while autonomy, engagement, and security showed no detected difference. Human advisors were valued for empathy and contextual judgment in complex decisions, whereas AI agents were valued for availability, efficiency, and emotional consistency. Rather than competing alternatives, these results point toward complementary systems that position agents as first-line support while preserving human connection for high-stakes, emotionally complex interactions.

While initial adoption marks the preliminary phase of Generative AI integration in higher education, long-term impact on learning relies heavily on students’ continuance intention. This Systematic Literature Review (SLR) investigates publication trajectories, theoretical frameworks, and contextual determinants to extend the Expectation Confirmation Model of Information Systems Continuance (ECM-ISC) within tertiary education. Following structured planning, execution, and reporting phases, a comprehensive search across Scopus, IEEE, and PubMed databases spanning 2021 to 2026 yielded 2,107 initial records, from which 31 peer-reviewed papers met strict eligibility and quality criteria. The analysis reveals an exponential rise in GenAI continuance research during 2025 and 2026. The theoretical frameworks commonly employed include TAM, ECM/ECT, UTAUT/UTAUT2, TTF, D&M IS Success Model, S-O-R, and hybrid SEM-ANN approaches. The main findings indicate that perceived information quality, trust, perceived risk, and intrinsic motivation are relevant external factors for extending ECM-ISC. Synthesizing these dimensions, this study delivers a refined ECM-ISC framework tailored to higher education, offering strategic insights for GenAI system design and institutional policymaking.

Objetivo. Sintetizar la evidencia sobre la inteligencia artificial (IA) en la educación, desde el origen del término (1955) hasta 2026, y analizar sus efectos en la salud cognitiva, mental y emocional de estudiantes y docentes, por nivel formativo.Método. Revisión integrativa según Whittemore y Knafl. Búsqueda sistematizada en PubMed el 27 de septiembre de 2026 (934 registros; 93 revisiones), complementada con búsqueda dirigida en arXiv, ACM, Nature, PNAS y literatura institucional, y rastreo de citas. Se incluyeron 23 fuentes empíricas o de síntesis y 14 documentos normativos e institucionales, jerarquizados por nivel de evidencia y analizados mediante síntesis temática y cuantitativa descriptiva.Resultados. El efecto de la IA depende del diseño pedagógico. Tutores con andamiaje produjeron ganancias de 0,23 a 0,31 desviaciones estándar (DE) en Nigeria y mayor aprendizaje en física universitaria. El acceso libre a GPT-4 redujo el desempeño 17 % al retirarlo. En lo cognitivo, la descarga cognitiva se asocia con menor pensamiento crítico y menor conectividad neural en escritura asistida (evidencia preliminar). En lo mental, la dependencia de IA generativa se asocia con ansiedad, depresión y agotamiento académico, mediados por menor autoeficacia. El uso diario intensivo de chatbots se asocia con soledad y dependencia emocional. Los chatbots basados en terapia cognitivo-conductual y las simulaciones clínicas muestran beneficios. La evidencia es escasa en formación técnica, tecnológica y de posgrado.Conclusiones. La IA funciona como andamio o como muleta según el diseño que la rodea. Se propone el Modelo de Andamiaje Protector y recomendaciones para la educación abierta y a distancia.

documents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded into applications, allowing users to complete tasks either through direct manipulation or by delegating actions to conversational agents. However, little is known about how users balance these modalities when both are available. We present a web-based content management system augmented with an LLM agent through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling users to perform CRUD tasks through a graphical interface, a conversational agent, or both. We conducted a between-subjects study (N=73) comparing three interaction modes: Traditional-Only, AI-First, and Hybrid. Across sixteen scenarios, we analyzed task completion time, interaction logs, and delegation behavior. AI-assisted interaction significantly reduced clicks, page navigations, and scrolling, indicating lower interaction effort. Surprisingly, these reductions did not translate into faster task completion, as task duration did not differ significantly across conditions. We also found no significant relationship between CRUD operation type and delegation, suggesting that users did not systematically avoid delegating higher-risk actions. Instead, delegation varied far more between participants than between tasks, with individual differences accounting for roughly half the variance in assistant use (ICC =.50). Our findings suggest that the primary benefit of human–agent interfaces may be reducing interaction effort rather than improving speed, and that delegation reflects who the user is more than what the task demands.

Purpose: This study investigated the factors that predict senior high school students' interest in and attitudes toward Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) education in Ghana. It examined how intrinsic motivation, self-determination, self-efficacy, career motivation, and grade motivation were linked to students' emotional engagement in STEM learning. Design/Methodology/Approach: This quantitative cross-sectional study used a structured questionnaire measured on a five-point Likert scale to collect data from 767 students. Students in Forms 1 to 3 were selected through proportional stratified sampling at three purposively selected senior high schools in the Greater Accra Region. Multiple regression analysis was used to identify the motivational factors that predict students’ interest in and attitude toward STEM. Research Limitation: This study is limited by its cross-sectional design, which restricts the ability to draw causal inferences. It also relied on self-reported data from students in one region of Ghana, which might limit its generalisability. Findings: The analysis showed that intrinsic motivation and self-determination strongly predict both STEM interest and attitudes. Self-efficacy and career motivation also predicted STEM interest but did not significantly predict attitude. In contrast, grade motivation predicts attitudes but not interest. The findings indicate that intrinsic motivation and self-determination are consistently associated with both STEM interest and STEM attitude, while other motivational factors show outcome-specific patterns. Practical Implication: The results suggest the need for educational changes that support student autonomy, promote inquiry-based learning, and improve career counselling. These changes can help connect teaching methods with motivational factors that maintain students’ interest and positive attitudes toward STEM. Social Implication: By highlighting the key psychological factors that drive STEM engagement, this study provides insights for policymakers looking to improve low STEM participation rates and encourage long-term economic development through more scientifically informed and skilled youth. Originality/Value: The findings indicate that STEM interest and attitudes reflect distinct motivational patterns. Intrinsic motivation and self-determination predict students’ STEM interest and STEM attitude, while self-efficacy and career motivation predict interest, and grade motivation predicts attitudes. It extends context-specific evidence and supports differentiated interpretations of STEM motivation.

Des utilisateurs soumettent désormais aux IA conversationnelles des conflits relationnels, des hésitations morales ou des décisions personnelles pour obtenir une validation avant d’agir. Cet article conceptualise comme réassurance algorithmique le recours à l’IA pour sortir de l’hésitation décisionnelle, état où l’information suffirait à décider mais où le sentiment de suffisance fait défaut. À partir d’une revue intégrative ciblée, nous soutenons que l’enjeu distinctif n’est pas la recherche de réassurance elle-même, mais une architecture de service qui la rend disponible, privée et presque sans friction sociale. Nous développons le mécanisme de délégation de la clôture décisionnelle : ce qui se déplace n’est pas la décision, mais le signal que la délibération peut s’arrêter. Le caractère intime de la demande explique en partie que la consultation se répète sans gain informationnel. Dans certains des contextes marocains, africains et arabes documentés ici, le conseil peut s’inscrire dans des relations peu substituables ; nous traitons cette configuration comme une variable à mesurer, non comme un trait culturel. Les propositions, non testées, sont assorties d’un agenda empirique et d’implications pour la conception des services conversationnels et la gouvernance des données intimes.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Wellness programs for employees are becoming essential in manufacturing since occupational health, work organization, physical demands, and psychosocial conditions can affect worker wellness and functional performance. This paper reviews the impact of programmes which enhance health in the workplace on productivity and job satisfaction in a manufacturing setting. A systematic critical assessment was conducted of peer-reviewed intervention studies, systematic reviews and authoritative occupational-health advice related specifically to Covid-19 pandemic and literature from 2020-2026 including relevant earlier studies. The existing body of research deals with both the promotion of physical health and risk management and stress management approaches. Programs that improve health behaviours, perceived wellbeing, work ability and other aspects of employee experience can be effective, according to the research. Nonetheless, the proof pertaining to absenteeism, objectively assessed output, and job satisfaction consistently shows improvement. The differences in study design, participant selection, duration of programme, measurement of outcome and context of industry prohibits direct comparisons and causality interpretation. The findings revealed that integrating individual support with risk mitigation can enhance the efficacy of wellness programs for manufacturing employees. In addition, supportive supervision, employee involvement, and execution consistent with shift schedules and production requirements are also favorable. The research also reveals that self-reported productivity as a proxy for verified production cannot address limitation and there are not enough rigorous longitudinal studies in manufacturing. Future studies should combine established job-satisfaction measurement instruments with objectively recorded measurement of output, quality, absence, and safety indicators, while also exploring programme costs, equity of access, and longer-term sustainability.

documents.abstract: The overarching goal of reinforcement learning (RL) is to efficiently optimize the agent's policy for various environments, tasks, dynamics, and even user preferences, which often consist of multiple and potentially conflicting rewards/objectives. This necessitates the learning of Pareto-optimal policies that can navigate different trade-offs among objectives. However, existing multi-objective RL (MORL) methods, whether trained online or offline, are typically limited to task- or objective-specific policy learning and do not address generalization of learned trade-offs to unseen tasks/objectives. In this work, we propose the Foundation Pareto Flow Policy (FP2) for offline MORL in continuous robotic control, inspired by the pre-mid-post-training paradigm underlying recent foundation models. Specifically, we instantiate FP2 as a multi-modal diffusion transformer equipped with a likelihood-free flow matching loss, enabling unified, scalable, and instructable learning of diverse trade-off trajectories. We further develop a three-stage training pipeline to gradually optimize the policy: (1) pre-training on a large-scale MORL dataset, (2) mid-training on a carefully curated high-quality dataset, and (3) post-training on few collected trajectory data from new tasks and trade-offs. Empirical results demonstrate that FP2 outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on most tasks of the D4MORL benchmark, achieving superior zero-shot interpolation and extrapolation on complex Pareto manifolds as well as efficient few-shot adaptation of the learned trade-off prior to new continuous-control tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/FibonacciRabbit/FP2.

Trust is central to human–agent interaction, but agentic AI raises a stronger question: when does perceived trust translate into delegated action? This poster introduces an agent-based simulation in which agents delegate when trust exceeds a threshold, observe success or failure, and update trust through outcome feedback with tunable failure sensitivity. We vary AI reliability and delegation thresholds while examining social conformity and failure sensitivity. Results show that unreliable systems drive abandonment, while intermediate regimes can produce apparent bistability: identical AI reliability can lead to adoption or rejection depending on initial trust and the delegation threshold. Conformity can sustain delegation by preventing isolated trust collapse. These findings suggest that delegation thresholds act as control parameters for sustained reliance. Future work will validate the model with human participants and heterogeneous agent profiles and tasks.

As AI systems gain agency in workplaces, workers increasingly interact with systems that do more than support tasks: they make decisions, allocate work, and shape how workers communicate with others. We interviewed 16 workers in healthcare, finance, and management about their daily interactions with workplace AI systems. Across these domains, AI occupied three agentic roles: assistant, supporting worker decision-making; arbiter, making consequential decisions that workers had to explain to downstream stakeholders; and manager, directing work and displacing social structures through which work had been negotiated and learned. We find that worker needs depended on how decision authority and accountability were configured around the AI system. Explanation, control, accountability, and communication each took different meanings depending on whether AI supported, decided, or directed work. We contribute a role-based account of workplace human-agent interaction and identify accountability-authority asymmetry as a mechanism through which AI deployments can place responsibility on workers for outcomes whose authority has shifted to AI. We discuss implications for designing workplace AI around both the agent and its surrounding agency configuration.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI can support learning, but it may also encourage cognitive outsourcing by replacing learners’ own thinking. This study reframes AI from an information provider to a responsive listener that promotes cognitive engagement and self-explanation. We introduce Hearble, a minimal robotic listener designed to isolate the effects of different backchannel modalities. Using a between-subjects design, we compare four conditions: no response, visual, nonverbal acoustic, and verbal backchannels. We examine how these conditions affect utterance elaboration, cognitive load, immediate comprehension, knowledge transfer, and perceived agency. Rather than limiting AI intervention to preserving learners’ cognitive processes, we investigate whether AI can actively support them by encouraging learners to articulate and elaborate their own thoughts. This work presents the physical AI listener as an alternative interaction paradigm for learning and provides a controlled foundation for future research on how embodiment, facial expressions, gestures, and other audience cues shape learning and agency.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: AI agents increasingly remember prior interactions and present themselves through distinct personalities. Whether these relational features help users calibrate their trust appropriately, or instead impose hidden costs without improving how well they rely on agent guidance, is an open and consequential design question. In a remote virtual reality study (N = 92), we independently varied whether an agent referenced its shared history with the user and whether its personality matched the user’s own style. Agents that made memory references caused users to slow down and deliberate longer at every decision point, yet this caution produced no improvement in compliance quality—a pattern we call the memory paradox. More social did not mean better calibrated. Personality congruence did not make users trust the agent more overall, but it did make their trust judgments more behaviorally coherent. Across all conditions, participants followed incorrect agent guidance at a strikingly high rate, and no relational design feature reduced this automation bias. Taken together, these findings argue that the core challenge in human-agent collaboration is not building trust, but calibrating it: AI agents should be evaluated by how accurately users rely on them, not by how humanlike they feel.

Explainability helps users assess evidence behind an AI recommendation, but it may not change decisions when that evidence goes unexamined. The problem is sharper in agentic decision support, where one assistant interprets evidence, explains its assessment, and recommends an action, while anthropomorphic delivery may add social credibility. Cognitive forcing, operationalised here as Human Intervention Checkpoints (HICs), requires users to specify what the assistant should examine before it recommends. We report a randomised 2 × 2 × 2 hiring experiment (N = 211) in which recruiters assessed a candidate whose unmet role-critical requirements were stated in every recommendation. Advancement was not associated with explanatory provenance, anthropomorphic delivery, HIC presence, or opening source documents. Post-task perceived explainability was associated with perceived anthropomorphism and trust, and trust was associated with advancement. In HIC-present conditions, 70 participants directed the assistant to a role-critical requirement and received Hold, yet 46 advanced. The findings identify a boundary of cognitive forcing: influence over what the agent evaluated and recommended did not reliably carry through to the final human decision.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Objective: This study describes how an Akidah Akhlak teacher applies a humanistic approach at State Islamic Senior High School (Madrasah Aliyah Negeri, MAN) 2 Klaten, Indonesia, and interprets how these practices may support the conditions for students’ love of science. Theoretical framework: The analysis draws on Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, Rogers’ person-centred learning, Freire’s dialogical education and Deci and Ryan’s self-determination theory, and treats hubb al-ʿilm as an Islamic educational orientation that overlaps with, but is not identical to, intrinsic motivation. Literature review: The literature review examines humanistic Islamic education through Maslow, Rogers, Freire, and self-determination theory, highlighting the relationship between student autonomy, emotional needs, moral learning, and hubb al-ʿilm. Research gap: Earlier studies of humanistic Akidah Akhlak learning have mostly examined primary-level madrasahs and moral outcomes such as courtesy and discipline, leaving field evidence on knowledge-oriented outcomes at the Madrasah Aliyah level limited. Methods: A qualitative case study used semi-structured interviews, passive participatory classroom observation and documentation review. Data were analyzed with the interactive model of Miles, Huberman and Saldaña, and credibility was supported by source triangulation and member checking. Results: Three interrelated strategies emerged: differentiating methods according to class conduciveness; negotiating relational agreements that recognize students’ basic needs and autonomy, namely a responsibility-based eating and drinking policy and the absence of homework; and responding to mistakes with mild consequences followed by reflective dialogue on the purpose of seeking knowledge. Together, these practices appear to create a low-threat climate that is conducive to curiosity and to a shift from external towards more internalized motivation. Because the evidence rests mainly on the teacher’s account, supported by classroom observation and documents, the study does not claim that students’ love of science was measured or has increased. Implications: The three-stage model offered here is a contextual interpretation of one case, and may inform teacher reflection and training in comparable madrasahs. Novelty: The study foregrounds hubb al-ʿilm as an affective orientation in humanistic Akidah Akhlak learning at the Madrasah Aliyah level and documents concrete relational agreements that are rarely reported.

Industrial emergencies in refineries, petroleum terminals, chemical plants, and other high-hazard facilities require more than effective firefighting, process isolation, and rescue operations. They also demand timely, accurate, coordinated and stakeholder-specific communication. When information is delayed, inconsistent or inaccessible, operational response may be impeded, families may experience avoidable distress, emergency access may be obstructed, and confidence in the organization may be weakened. This paper examines three practitioner-observed industrial fire emergencies: a refinery fire/explosion in 1988, a fire at Jawahar Dweep in 2017, and a fire emergency encountered during an occupational health, safety, and environment audit. The cases are used as retrospective practitioner illustrations rather than as a statistically representative or conventionally documented qualitative dataset. The paper distinguishes direct observations and recollections from interpretations informed by emergency-communication literature and from the managerial framework proposed by the author. It develops an Industrial Crisis Communication Framework covering preparedness, detection and notification, command and information verification, stakeholder-specific dissemination, monitoring and feedback, and post-emergency learning. Attention is given to family information arrangements, communication redundancy, the separation of operational command channels from public-facing communication, vulnerable stakeholders, misinformation, cyber resilience, and measurable readiness. A preliminary readiness scorecard is proposed for pilot testing in tabletop and full-scale exercises. The framework is intended as a practical, auditable aid for plant-specific emergency preparedness; its effectiveness requires prospective validation.

Multicultural education in Hong Kong poses learning challenges. For example, non-Chinese-speaking (NCS) students and newly-arrived students (NAS) come from diverse linguistic backgrounds. However, existing interventions emphasise unidirectional instruction. This study addresses the gap by investigating how an interactive robot-assisted scenario (RAS) system can support Cantonese instruction in multicultural classrooms. We employ a mixed-method approach examining quantitative engagement measures and qualitative experiential data. We investigate how RAS intervention can influence the engagement and motivation of NAS and NCS students to learn Cantonese, and the impacts of RAS on the Cantonese proficiency outcomes of NAS and NCS learners. Findings reveal differential engagement patterns: NAS demonstrate improvements in behavioural engagement, while NCS students show a slight decline in cognitive engagement. This research contributes to human-agent interaction (HAI) by examining cross-cultural learning dynamics and providing preliminary insights for the development of multicultural educational technologies.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This systematic review examines interventions designed to regulate cognitive offloading to generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and their effects on subsequent independent performance in educational and employee development contexts. The review aims to identify how interventions structure the distribution of cognitive work between individuals and GenAI, evaluate their effects on learning and task performance after AI assistance has been withdrawn, and examine the conditions under which these effects may differ. Eligible evidence will include comparative experimental and quasi-experimental studies assessing independent knowledge, skills or task performance following GenAI-supported activities. Electronic searches were conducted in six bibliographic databases and preprint repositories, followed by deduplication and pilot screening. Two reviewers will independently screen studies and extract data. The review will use structured descriptive synthesis, supplemented by meta-analysis where the evidence permits. Risk of bias will be assessed using JBI tools, and certainty of evidence for key outcomes will be evaluated using GRADE. The expected contribution is an evidence-based understanding of which approaches to regulating cognitive offloading have been evaluated, what effects they produce on independent performance, and how confidently these effects can be interpreted. Findings may inform the design of GenAI-supported education and employee development activities.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated judges for AI-generated content, yet a single judge is unreliable and even a panel of judges leaves a hard residue: when judges disagree, majority voting simply discards the conflict instead of resolving it. We present JuryFlow, a disagreement-guided, human-in-the-loop multi-agent evaluation framework that treats inter-judge disagreement not as noise to be averaged away, but as a precise, claim-level signal indicating where an evaluation is uncertain. JuryFlow decomposes each candidate response into atomic claims, has a panel of heterogeneous judges assign per-claim verdicts, and builds a disagreement graph whose nodes are scored by verdict entropy and whose edges encode structural similarity between claims. A human acts as a structural guide, i.e., selecting which disagreement to resolve through a single, minimal intervention rather than re-labeling the response, after which the focal claim is re-evaluated, the correction propagates along graph edges and to historically similar cases, and is crystallized into reusable rubric entries that all judges inherit, making the evaluator progressively self-refining. To enable large-scale, reproducible benchmarking without human studies, we evaluate JuryFlow in an automatic configuration in which the focal selection is made by entropy ranking. On MT-Bench and LLMBar, JuryFlow improves agreement with gold labels over single-judge and majority-vote panel baselines, and ablations isolate the contributions of disagreement-targeted re-evaluation, propagation, and rubric induction. We contribute (1) a human-in-the-loop paradigm that recasts the human from labeler to structural guide, (2) the JuryFlow framework operationalizing it through a disagreement graph, focal re-evaluation, and closed-loop rubric induction, and (3) an evaluation protocol with ablations that isolate where the gains originate.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: There is growing interest in understanding how people interact with large language models (LLMs) and whether such models elicit dependency or even addictive behaviour. Validated tools to assess the extent to which individuals may become dependent on LLMs are scarce and primarily build on classic behavioural addiction symptoms, adapted to the context of LLM use. We view this as a conceptual limitation, as the LLM-human relationship is more nuanced and warrants a fresh and distinct perspective. To address this gap, we developed and validated a new 12-item questionnaire to measure LLM dependency, referred to as LLM-D12. The scale was based on the authors’ prior theoretical work, with items developed accordingly and responses collected from 526 participants in the UK. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, performed on separate halves of the total sample using a split-sample approach, supported a two-factor structure: Instrumental Dependency (six items) and Relationship Dependency (six items). Instrumental Dependency reflects the extent to which individuals rely on LLMs to support or collaborate in decision-making and cognitive tasks. Relationship Dependency captures the tendency to perceive LLMs as socially meaningful, sentient, or companion-like entities. The two-factor structure demonstrated excellent internal consistency and clear discriminant validity. External validation confirmed both the conceptual foundation and the distinction between the two subscales. The psychometric properties and structure of our LLM-D12 scale were interpreted in light of the emerging view that dependency on LLMs does not necessarily indicate dysfunction but may still reflect reliance levels that could become problematic in certain contexts.

Evaluating whether an AI agent behaves like a good teammate is becoming a bottleneck as multi-agent language-model systems proliferate, because human ratings do not scale to the transcripts these systems generate. We ask whether a language model can stand in for a human rater of teammate quality, offering a controlled proof-of-concept validation rather than a large-scale study. Drawing on the autonomous-agent teammate-likeness construct from the human-autonomy-teaming literature, we define a six-dimension behavioral coding scheme covering altruistic, benevolent, interdependent, emotive, communicative, and synchronized conduct, adapted for a language-model judge. We validate it by rewriting the partner’s lines in team-task transcripts as cooperative, neutral, or defective while holding the rest fixed, and having five judges from five model families rate every version. Every judge orders the manipulated behavior as intended and every pair agrees on relative ordering, though absolute calibration differs by up to about a scale point. On registers matched for length and politeness the judges separate cooperative from degraded conduct but resolve subtle defection only weakly; a blinded single-rater human pilot reproduces both the orderings and that limit. The scheme is therefore valid for relative comparisons but not for absolute thresholds applied across judges. We give design implications for LLM-judge teaming evaluation, and release the scheme, stimuli, prompts, and ratings.

Digital Twin (DT) systems are increasingly applied to domestic energy management, distributing decision-making across sensors, algorithms, and users. Designing for shared agency requires making this distribution explicit. This paper characterises engagement in domestic DTs through two lenses: Digital Twin Engagement Style (Visibility × Proactivity) and User Engagement Style (Intentionality × Activeness). These dimensions make system initiative, information visibility, user intentions, and behavioral activity designable. The framework helps designers identify alignments and tensions between user and system engagement, and trace how agency shifts across interaction configurations. Future work will apply the framework to design cases to develop concrete guidelines and assess its practical usefulness.

Purpose This study tests a dual-process Self-Determination Theory (SDT) model in L2 classrooms by examining engagement and disengagement concurrently, retaining their multidimensional structures, and investigating their higher-order and facet-level associations with end-of-course …

Conversational AI often places navigation cost on users by requiring them to continuously steer conversations, articulate preferences, and monitor AI responses. Reducing this cost may require giving AI systems more conversational initiative, raising questions about how this shift affects users’ agency and responsibility. We explore a 2-on-1 AI deliberation design, where users overhear two agents’ discussion and intervene when needed. Informed by a formative study, our system pairs a Personalized AI representing the user’s preferences with an Expert AI providing alternative perspectives. In a within-subjects mixed-methods study on travel planning, 2-on-1 deliberation reduced navigation cost and perceived agency, while we observed no statistically detectable difference in decision responsibility across conditions. Qualitative findings suggest that users shifted from steering the conversation to overhearing, evaluating, and selectively intervening in agent-to-agent deliberation. We discuss overhearing as an evaluative mode of participation in AI deliberation systems.

In AI-assisted decision-making, achieving warranted trust is essential: users should follow accurate advice while rejecting wrong suggestions. But as LLM-based AI agents reshape decision support, such agents often display miscalibrated confidence – ranging from confidently incorrect hallucinations to overly non-committal hedging. To understand how this behavior and unannounced system changes impact user trust, we conducted a two-phase online study (N=90) evaluating advice-seeking and reliance after confidence calibration is silently updated. We found that users’ willingness to seek AI advice is driven overwhelmingly by their pre-existing (positive) attitudes toward AI, not by the system’s prior performance. However, once they actively consult the AI, their reliance is significantly higher if they previously encountered a confidently incorrect or a non-committal system rather than a calibrated baseline. This effect dampens over time, with qualitative insights showing how unannounced background changes can erode perceived quality. These findings demonstrate that safe AI integration requires addressing individual user biases and transparently communicating updates.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: University students occasionally struggle to ask questions in class. While AI can support learning, little is known about how it can support in-class question asking. We developed an AI system that generates questions in real time from lecture content and a mobile interface that allows students to view, vote on, and submit their own questions alongside AI-generated ones. We deployed this system in four computer-science lectures, and found that AI-generated questions helped students consider lecture content from different perspectives. For some, this prompted deeper reflection on what to ask. However, others reported reduced motivation to form their own questions, suggesting risks of overreliance. Although students found the AI helpful, they more frequently voted for questions asked by their peers, revealing a gap between AI-generated questions and students’ in-the-moment learning needs. We provide design recommendations for systems that promote interactive collaboration with AI and scaffold question asking without undermining student agency.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: While HCI has expanded from Personal to Family Informatics, researchers still lack a critical analytical vocabulary to diagnose what truly constitutes a collective care context. We introduce Sangyadhi, an analytical sociotechnical framework that synthesizes Situated Action, Distributed Cognition, the Capabilities Approach, and Actor-Network Theory to investigate multi-actor care ecologies. The framework articulates four interdependent analytical lenses: contextual grounding, distributed responsibility, trust-mediated sharing, and collaborative actionability. To demonstrate its diagnostic utility, we apply Sangyadhi to critically audit a decade of HCI digital health literature across self-tracking, family informatics, and clinical AI---surfacing structural omissions in how shifting authority, dynamic trust, and AI escalation are conceptualized. Ultimately, the goal of Sangyadhi is to equip researchers with an analytical blueprint for diagnosing observed care contexts, structuring field inquiries, and evaluating future technologies.

Objective: To analyze the effects of Integrative Community Therapy (ICT) on self-perceived happiness and emotional well-being among slaughterhouse workers in a Brazilian municipality located on an international border. Methods: This exploratory quasi-experimental study was grounded in the ICT framework and conducted in Itaipulândia, Paraná, from April to December 2019. The McDowell and Newell Faces Scale was used to assess self-perceived happiness before and after ICT circles, alongside a sociodemographic questionnaire and an analysis of universal themes and coping strategies that emerged during the circles. Results: Twelve circles were held with 151 workers. Self-perceived happiness and emotional state improved significantly after the circles. The main universal themes were physical health problems, bereavement, family conflict, and stress, revealing the connection between emotional suffering and the work context. The most common coping strategies were seeking spiritual or religious support, strengthening family relationships, and personal empowerment. Workers aged 18–24 years had 4.28 times greater odds of emotional improvement after participating in the circles than workers older than 24 years. Conclusion: ICT showed promise as a relationship-centered care strategy in occupational health, supporting improved self-perceived happiness and emotional well-being and strengthening support networks among slaughterhouse workers. Collective and integrative care strategies may be particularly valuable in work settings marked by physical and psychosocial vulnerability.

Students are adopting LLMs at scale. This poses a question: does unrestricted AI access bypass the cognitive effort required for learning, or does it streamline knowledge acquisition? This paper reports on a study where we compare three designs for user-AI interaction in a learning context: (1) an unrestricted conversational bot like ChatGPT, (2) a pedagogically constrained bot that guides through hints without giving final answers, which we refer to as the Socratic mode; and (3) a non-conversational adaptive tutoring system that adjusts difficulty in real-time based on the user’s cognitive engagement derived from the brain signals. Fifty study participants were tasked with learning about nuclear safety protocols, a domain chosen for its zero-prior knowledge baseline. The participants progressed through an instructional video, a pre-test, an AI-driven assessment phase, which varied in the three conditions, and an immediate post-test. The nature of the questions centered primarily on factual knowledge acquisition, but it still required participants to have a global understanding of the concepts in order to answer the questions correctly. A Muse headband was used to derive the cognitive engagement of all users in all conditions. The unrestricted chatbot produced higher learning gains (delta) than both constrained modes ( p <.03, d > 0.80), while the adaptive condition generated significantly higher EEG engagement ( p =.018). The cluster analysis of chatbot usage and discussion patterns by users showed that most participants in the unrestricted-mode adopted a direct answer-retrieval strategy, while participants in the Socratic-mode initially attempted to reason through the hints before progressively disengaging. Consequently, this also suggests that the success of the unrestricted AI is not an evidence of deeper learning, but rather a result of the immediate post-test evaluation after the training phase.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Applied studies of employee performance in Indonesian technical firms usually ask which factor dominates. This study asks instead whether technical competence, occupational health and safety (OHS), and the work environment behave as rival levers or as a bundle of resources. A census survey of all 41 employees of PT Multi Jaya Teknik, an electrical and mechanical contractor in Batu Bara Regency, North Sumatra, measured each construct with a five-item Likert scale (α = .807-.903), and performance was regressed on the three predictors by ordinary least squares. The predictors jointly explained a large share of variance, R² = .602 (adjusted R² = .570), F(3, 37) = 18.65, p < .001. Technical competence (B = 0.372, 95% CI [0.035, 0.709], f² = 0.135), OHS (B = 0.290, 95% CI [0.048, 0.532], f² = 0.159), and work environment (B = 0.261, 95% CI [0.018, 0.504], f² = 0.127) each retained a unique positive association, with closely matched standardized weights (β = .267-.335) and overlapping intervals. Because the smallest individual effect the design could detect was f² = 0.202, each estimate is individually fragile, whereas the joint effect is clear. The pattern is interpreted as safe competence: in hazardous field work, capability, safety provision, and workable conditions act as non-redundant resources, so no single lever should be expected to dominate. The study also shows that perceived OHS provision predicts self-rated performance, not accident prevention, and it offers a complete reporting template for small single-firm samples.

What people hand over to an AI agent has a boundary: a point at which advice becomes action taken on their behalf. We examine that distinction across six agent scenarios rated by 296 U.S. adults, analyzed as 3 (domain) × 2 (advisory versus substitutive). Advisory scenarios received higher ratings in each domain, with a larger partial η2 for scenario category than for domain (.465 versus.053). The contrast was positive in every subgroup examined, but domain-specific differences showed low internal consistency (α =.08), giving limited support for a single cross-domain tendency. Objective AI knowledge and awareness of model limitations were associated with overall willingness in opposite directions. These vignette contrasts do not isolate a causal effect of retained override.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Hospitals and health systems are complex adaptive systems. Safe care, continuity of services and the ability to adapt under pressure all depend on people noticing what is happening, making sense of it and anticipating what comes next. Situational awareness (SA), a concept that grew out of military aviation and human factors engineering, is now built into clinical non-technical skills frameworks, organisational resilience models and crisis management practice.

This article asks how a scientific, evidence-generating approach can speed up the adoption of artificial intelligence in healthcare. We use LifeLink Monitoring as an applied case and combine a structured literature review, market and regulatory analysis, competitive benchmarking, stakeholder surveys and expert interviews, scenario modelling, and pilot design. The analysis reveals a persistent shortage of context-specific evidence on clinical utility, workflow integration, human factors, economics, and governance. To address it, we propose an Evidence-to-Adoption Framework in which staged pilots turn technological hypotheses into evidence that clinicians, managers, regulators, payers, and investors can act on. We treat acceleration as a proposed mechanism that requires prospective testing, not as a demonstrated outcome, and we specify how it can be measured.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Technology and Human Factors in Education and Health

documents.abstract: Unsignalized roundabouts remain challenging for connected and autonomous vehicles because of dynamic merges, spatial conflicts, and communication constraints. We present a decentralized coordination architecture based on Group Mutual Exclusion (GME), in which each conflict point is treated as a local critical section and compatible virtual platoons may be admitted concurrently. A lead vehicle aggregates requests from its physical queue and relays admission decisions to following vehicles. To make this safety-critical process intelligible to occupants, we introduce a query-driven small language model (SLM) interface that reads structured controller traces and produces explanations only when requested. The SLM is strictly read-only and cannot alter GME decisions. We illustrate how traces containing conflict, priority, and waiting-time information can support contextual explanations of yielding, deceleration, and merging. The work provides an architecture and feasibility demonstration. Quantitative traffic, language-model, and human-factors evaluations are left to future work.

Reliance on artificial agents involves at least two decisions: whether to use the system and whether to verify its output. We examined how trust and self-reported verification fatigue were associated with these dimensions in survey responses from 390 adults across six English-speaking countries. Trust was strongly associated with AI use frequency (β =.50), whereas verification fatigue was not (β =.05). Fatigue was instead associated with verification skipping (β =.36) and selective verification (β =.31) but not reliably with active verification, and these two coefficients did not differ (Δβ =.05, p =.382). Trust was associated only with skipping among the three effort-graded verification behaviors, and its coefficient was larger for skipping than for selective verification (Δβ =.12, p =.040). No interaction survived correction. This pattern is consistent with trust relating to perceived verification necessity and self-reported verification fatigue to perceived verification burden, two routes converging on verification skipping; however, the cross-sectional self-report design cannot establish these mechanisms.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) could make personalized tutoring available at scale, but it remains unclear how they can best support the instructional processes that make one-on-one instruction effective. We compared two ways of using LLMs after students make errors: providing personalized explanations of those errors, or engaging students in additional cycles of scaffolded practice and feedback, with a Socratic tutor guiding students toward the correct answer. In a preregistered online experiment, 400 adults practiced setting up constraint equations and, after each attempt, received the correct answer, a generic explanation, a personalized LLM explanation of their error, or Socratic tutoring. Socratic tutoring helped: participants resolved 64% of their errors through the dialogue and scored 0.24 SD higher on practice-aligned posttest questions than those who received generic or personalized explanations. Socratic participants also found the session more interesting, less frustrating, and less costly, even though it took nearly twice as long. In contrast, we found no evidence of a benefit of personalized explanations over generic ones, and neither type of explanation reliably outperformed simply seeing the correct answer. These findings suggest that LLM tutors may add the most value not by explaining errors more precisely but by helping students correct those errors themselves through scaffolded practice. This pattern fits a mastery-experience account of tutoring, in which an effective tutor notices when a student is struggling, steps in with guidance, and works with the student until the struggle resolves into success. AI tutors may be most effective when designed around this principle.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into healthcare systems, from clinical information retrieval to workflow automation and decision support, which introduces new security, privacy, and trust risks with direct implications for patient care. While prior work has examined these risks from technical and regulatory perspectives, less is known about how these risks are naturally discussed in online communities. To address this gap, we conduct a large-scale analysis of 14 medical communities on Reddit and extract 6,514 relevant posts. Through systematic qualitative coding and LLM-assisted classification, we investigate concerns expressed in healthcare AI discussions, their prevalence, and how they evolve over time. Our analysis reveals that users perceive healthcare AI as expanding traditional healthcare trust boundaries and attack surfaces through integrations with electronic health records, third-party services, cloud platforms, and automated clinical workflows. Posts express concerns about over-privileged access to sensitive records, opaque data flows, unauthorized secondary use, and unsafe automation can amplify the consequences of errors and misuse. We identify four attitudes toward these risks: exploring questions of accountability and harm, cautiously accepting AI with stronger safeguards, skepticism about system trustworthiness, and resignation to growing data exposure and automation. Longitudinal analysis shows that SP&T discussions have increased significantly, with shifts coinciding with major healthcare AI deployments, privacy incidents, and regulatory developments. These findings illuminate changing trust relationships and data-governance challenges, informing the design and governance of safer, more transparent, and accountable healthcare AI systems.

Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Recent advances in large language models allow a working application to be generated from natural-language description, and is referred to as generative user interfaces. Their application to behavior change is unexplored, and we provide one of the first controlled investigations of it. We distinguish two components of authorship: iteration, the revision of a generated artifact in natural language, and personalization, the conditioning of generation on stated context. In a pre-registered between-subjects experiment (N = 300, 60 per condition), we crossed these two factors and added a static intervention as a control, yielding five conditions; participants stated a goal and received a generated intervention. The personalized generative condition ranked highest on every self-report outcome, including ownership, satisfaction, and intended adoption. Randomized iteration had no detectable effect, and higher revision counts were negatively associated with evaluative ratings. This work establishes which component of authorship carries motivational value in generative behavior change tools.

A basic AI label reveals that AI was involved but says little about how the resulting advice was produced or reviewed. This study tests a first-stage moderated mediation model in which transparency messages relate to self-reported willingness to follow AI-mediated financial advice through perceived trustworthiness, conditional on AI role. In a six-condition between-subjects experiment (N = 227), participants received the same portfolio recommendation across three transparency conditions (no disclosure, basic AI disclosure, and detailed explanation) and two AI-role framings (primary source and support tool). The no-disclosure conditions formed a common participant-facing baseline in which AI role was not communicated. Within the support-tool reference condition, basic disclosure did not increase perceived trustworthiness relative to no disclosure, whereas the detailed message increased trustworthiness relative to both no disclosure and basic disclosure. Perceived trustworthiness was strongly associated with willingness to follow the recommendation (b = 1.018, p <.001). The detailed-message × AI-role interaction was significant (b = −.291, 95% CI [ −.450, −.132]), and the detailed-versus-no-disclosure indirect effect through trustworthiness excluded zero in the support-tool condition (indirect effect =.504, 95% bootstrap CI [.032,.976]) but not in the primary-source condition. Because the detailed messages also differed in whether human review was present, the interaction captures differences between advisory-message configurations rather than a pure effect of explanation depth or AI role. The findings advance a content-sensitive account of AI transparency: labels alone were insufficient, while what transparency communicated about advice production, decision authority, and human review was consequential for trustworthiness judgments and willingness to follow AI-mediated advice.

Children increasingly use AI agents that can act on their own. Yet, many agentic systems are designed around a capable user, one who can judge a response, absorb an error, and speak up for their own needs, and who thereby serves as the final check on an overstepping system. A child user is not a small adult [29], and children’s ability to interpret and rely on an agent is still developing. Systems that rely on the child’s judgment as their source of human oversight therefore pose real dangers in exactly the moments that matter most [25, 28]. We propose that the agent can supply this check, and refer the child to a trusted adult. This action complements existing methods such as content-based refusal, confidence-based abstention, fixed age-gating, and emotional-safety filtering. Beyond asking whether a request is permissible or an answer confident, the agent also asks whether the situation is one it should handle alone. Taking the developing child into consideration, we identify the circumstances in which an agent should not act alone and specify the response each calls for. These situations form the basis of a research agenda that we plan to develop into benchmarks and design resources for child-facing agents.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study examines the perceived credibility of AI- versus human-written news. A 3×2×2 online experiment (N = 480) finds that human-written and human–AI collaborative news are rated more credible than AI-generated news, mediated by perceived accountability; media type and news type did not moderate the effects. The study informs trust in human–machine journalism and responsible AI use.
topics: News Media Framing and Political Communication

documents.abstract: As social agents, robots, conversational AI systems, and virtual characters become embedded in everyday environments, HAI is shifting from isolated one-human/one-agent interaction toward socially embedded multi-person and multi-agent settings. This workshop explores how trust, blame, and responsibility emerge, become distributed, and are negotiated among users, agents, developers, institutions, bystanders, and broader social contexts. We focus on agents as social participants in complex environments, including group dynamics, psychological safety, agent refusal, moral consideration, and legal or governance questions. The workshop aims to develop a preliminary issue map, research agenda, and interdisciplinary network for socially sustainable human-agent societies.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: As teleoperated systems increasingly incorporate autonomous agents capable of independent decision-making, the human operator transitions from a direct controller to a delegated supervisor. This shift introduces a fundamental challenge: how operators calibrate their trust toward agents whose decisions they cannot interpret. Miscalibrated trust, whether overtrust leading to unsafe delegation or undertrust causing inefficient over-intervention, represents one of the most consequential human factors risks in agentic teleoperation. This paper argues that Explainable AI (XAI) mechanisms constitute a promising but underexplored lever for dynamic trust calibration in teleoperated human-agent systems. A three-layer conceptual framework is proposed that maps operator profiles to adaptive XAI modality selection and closes the loop through a trust feedback mechanism that dynamically adjusts the agent’s level of autonomy. Three application scenarios, namely robotic surgical assistance, hazardous environment inspection, and remote industrial maintenance, are examined to illustrate how the framework operates under realistic teleoperation constraints. The paper identifies key research challenges and outlines a forward-looking agenda for empirically grounding the proposed framework.

рассматривается практическая задача распределения функций между студентом, преподавателем и генеративной моделью. Предложена модель трёх контуров делегирования — инструментального, тьюторского и партнёрского — а также четыре критерия выбора контура и принципы проектирования заданий и оценивания, снижающие риск утраты формируемого навыка. Приведён рабочий чек-лист преподавателя.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can now perform many academic tasks that students were once required to master, raising the question of whether learners still value learning for themselves and feel capable of learning without relying on AI. Available scales mainly focus on AI as the outcome of learning rather than the context of it. This study developed and validated brief scales measuring Learning Value in the Context of AI (LV-AI, the value of personally learning when associated tasks can be performed by AI) and Learning Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI (LSE-AI, the appraisal of ability to learn and perform academically without relying on AI) and examined their associations with AI use and academic outcomes (effort expenditure, persistence, GPA). Data were collected from 882 undergraduate students in the U.S. with approximately equal traditional-age and adult learners. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis supported a correlated two-factor structure. Both scales showed acceptable reliability (ω = .81 and .72), discriminant validity from classical task value and self-efficacy, and measurement invariance across student age type. When classical task value, classical self-efficacy, and AI use were controlled, LV-AI and LSE-AI incrementally predicted effort and persistence, but not GPA. Moreover, although AI use showed a significant negative association with academic effort, an exploratory mediation analysis indicated that this association no longer held when learners' LV-AI and LSE-AI were accounted for, with the indirect path carrying over half of the initial association. This highlights the important role these AI-embedded constructs play in preventing the disengagement tendencies.
